opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most interesting open problems right now. The way I frame it is: context length is a bit like working memory, and humans don't do long projects by holding everything in working memory either. We take notes, we write things down, we come back the next morning and re-read where we left off. So a lot of the challenge is really about teaching models to manage their own state well.

There are a few pieces to it. One is compaction or summarization: when you're getting close to the limit, can the model distill what actually matters? What's been tried, what failed, what the current hypothesis is, which files are relevant. The hard part is that the model doesn't always know in advance what will turn out to be important later, so you can lose a crucial detail that seemed minor at the time.

The second piece is external memory: giving the agent a scratchpad, a progress file, a to-do list, or just letting it lean on the environment itself. In coding that's actually really natural, because the codebase *is* the state. Git history, test results, comments, all of that is a memory the agent can re-read rather than having to carry in context. Some of the best results I've seen come from just encouraging the model to write good notes for its future self, almost like handing off to a coworker.

And then there's the evaluation and training side, which I think is underrated. It's hard to build environments where the task genuinely requires many context windows, and where you can tell whether the agent kept making real progress or just looped, or slowly drifted from the original goal. Coherence over long horizons is a different skill from being smart within a single window. You need the model to stay on task, notice when it's stuck, and not, say, quietly redefine the goal into something easier.

So I'd say the frontier isn't only about making context windows bigger, though that helps. It's about getting models to be good at the meta-skill of managing their own memory and progress, the way an experienced engineer manages a multi-week project.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls this one of the most interesting open problems and describes memory mechanisms such as summarization and external notes that help agents work across context windows.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, I think this is one of the most interesting open problems in agents right now. The way I frame it internally is: context is working memory, and no matter how long you make it, a real task eventually outgrows it. A human engineer working on a project for a week doesn't hold every file they've read in their head. They have notes, they have the codebase itself, they have git history, and they re-derive things as needed. So the question isn't really "how do we make context infinite," it's "how do we make the agent good at managing its own memory."

A few things we've found matter a lot. The first is summarization and compaction, which sounds boring but is actually hard to do well. When you compress a long trajectory, the model has to decide what's going to matter later, and it's easy to lose exactly the detail that turns out to be load-bearing. So a lot of the research is about getting the model to write summaries that are useful to a future version of itself that hasn't seen the original context. That's a weird skill. It's not just "summarize this," it's "write the note you'd want to find."

The second is externalizing state into the environment. Claude Code writes files, uses the filesystem, leaves scratchpads. The environment becomes the memory. And this actually generalizes really well, because the agent already knows how to read and write files, so you don't need a bespoke memory architecture. You just need the model to have good habits about when to write things down.

The third, and this is the one I find most interesting from a research perspective, is that a lot of long-horizon failures aren't really about context at all. They're about the model losing the thread of what it was trying to do. It gets deep into some rabbit hole, context fills up, and when it comes back it's forgotten the original goal or made a bad assumption that compounds. So part of the work is just making the model robust to its own context getting messy, teaching it to re-ground itself, check the plan, verify before acting.

And then there's evaluation, which is honestly the bottleneck. It's really hard to build evals for tasks that take hours or days. You can't just check a final answer. You end up needing environments where you can measure whether the agent made steady progress, recovered from mistakes, and didn't quietly drift. We've spent a surprising amount of effort just on that.

So I'd say the honest answer is: longer context helps and we keep pushing on it, but the real unlock is making the agent a good manager of its own attention. That's the part that feels like it'll matter even when context windows are ten times bigger than today.

r001.rationale: The response calls this an open problem and frames the research challenge as helping agents manage memory beyond their context, describing compaction, externalizing state, and re-grounding.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting challenge is that a longer context window only gets you so far. If you want an agent to work on something for days or weeks, eventually it needs to decide what to remember, what to write down, and what it can afford to forget.

And that’s harder than just summarizing the conversation. Suppose the agent tries three approaches and they all fail. You want it to preserve why they failed, or the next time it picks up the task, it might repeat exactly the same work. But if it preserves every detail, you’re back to filling up the context window. So the question is: what information will actually be useful for the next decision? Some of that you only discover later.

I’d think about that as a combination of memory and learning to manage your own working state. Can the agent leave itself a useful handoff? Can it retrieve the right evidence when it needs it? Can it recognize that its notes are stale? And then you need evaluations where losing that information actually matters—where the agent has to make progress across multiple context windows, rather than just answer a question about something it saw a long time ago.

r001.rationale: The response frames memory for work lasting beyond the context window as an unresolved challenge, discussing what agents should retain, write down, forget, and retrieve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the interesting challenge is that working beyond the context window isn’t just about making the window bigger. It’s about deciding what information you carry forward. If an agent spends a long time on a task, it needs to preserve the goal, what it’s learned, what it’s tried, and enough of the reasoning behind those decisions that it doesn’t repeat the same mistakes.

You can summarize the conversation, but summarization is lossy. Something that looks irrelevant now might become important later. So you probably want a combination of a compact working context and the ability to go back and retrieve the original details. For a coding agent, a lot of that memory can live in the environment itself: the code, tests, and notes about what remains to be done.

The research question is whether the agent can manage that process reliably. Can it recognize what it’s going to need later? Can it recover when its summary leaves something out? And can it pick up after a context reset without drifting away from the original task? That feels like a more useful target than simply asking how many tokens we can fit into a single call.

r001.rationale: The response describes carrying forward goals and learned information, combining summaries with retrieval of original details, and asks whether agents can manage this memory process reliably—framing it as a research question.
